intro: Ten cases that get harder as you go: painful bone metastases, cord compression, benign disease (Dupuytren, heterotopic ossification), impending fracture, SVC syndrome, trigeminal neuralgia, an AVM, prophylactic and oligometastatic radiation, and a goals-of-care consult at the end of life. Each starts with a one-liner, then gives you more information step by step: the imaging, the scores that decide the plan, the fractionation, the landmark trials, and what to tell the patient. Some steps are multiple choice, some are fill-in-the-blank.

cases.title: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours
cases.oneLiner: A 74-year-old man with castration-resistant prostate cancer has 3 weeks of aching right hip pain that keeps him up at night. He lives 2 hours from the cancer center. ECOG 2.

steps.label: Imaging
steps.caption: Whole-body Tc-99m bone scans from other patients: normal (left), multiple metastases (middle), and a superscan (right). Qureshi AM et al., World J Nucl Med 2017 (PMC5314659), CC BY-NC-SA.
steps.prompt: His bone scan is shown. What kind of metastases does prostate cancer usually cause, and why does the bone scan show them so well?
choices: Blastic (bone-forming), because the tracer collects where new bone is being made
Purely marrow-based, so the scan is usually negative
Lytic, because the scan detects bone destruction
steps.explanation: Prostate cancer is the classic blastic metastasis. Bone scan tracer is taken up where bone is being formed, so blastic lesions light up. Purely lytic lesions (myeloma especially) can be missed.

steps.label: Before you plan
steps.prompt: Pelvic X-rays and CT show a blastic lesion in the right ilium above the acetabulum with no cortical destruction. His pain is worse at night and better with dexamethasone. What do you need to rule out before planning simple palliative RT?
choices: Nothing; he can go straight to treatment
steps.explanation: An uncomplicated bone metastasis means no impending fracture, no cord or nerve compression, and no prior surgery to the site. Night pain that steroids help is biologic pain from the tumor, which responds well to RT.

steps.label: Fractionation
steps.prompt: Which course makes the most sense for him?
steps.explanation: For an uncomplicated painful bone metastasis, single and multiple fractions give the same pain relief. One visit matters for a man with limited performance status who lives far away.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that 8 Gy in 1 relieved pain as well as 30 Gy in 10 in breast and prostate cancer bone metastases?
steps.explanation: RTOG 9714: equal pain relief, less acute toxicity, and more retreatment after the single fraction.

steps.label: Counseling
steps.prompt: What do you tell him to expect?
steps.answer: Pain usually starts improving in 1-2 weeks and is best at about 4-6 weeks, so keep taking pain medicine until then. A temporary pain flare in the first few days is common, and dexamethasone lowers that risk. Fatigue is mild. About 1 in 5 patients need retreatment later.
steps.explanation: Dexamethasone around treatment reduced pain flare in NCIC SC.23.

steps.label: Three months later
steps.prompt: Three months later the hip pain returns, and a new scan shows many more painful bone metastases. He has no visceral disease. Besides more spot radiation, which systemic radiation treatment improved survival in this setting?
steps.explanation: Radium-223, an alpha emitter that behaves like calcium, improved overall survival in castration-resistant prostate cancer with symptomatic bone metastases and no visceral disease (ALSYMPCA). Strontium and samarium relieve pain only.

cases.title: Case 2: Tripping on the Stairs
cases.oneLiner: A 63-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer calls with 4 weeks of mid-back pain. Over the last 2 days she has been tripping on the stairs and her legs feel heavy.

steps.label: First orders
steps.prompt: What are your first two orders?
steps.answer: Dexamethasone (for example a 10 mg IV load, then 16 mg a day in divided doses) and an MRI of the whole spine, today.
steps.explanation: New back pain plus a neurologic change in a patient with cancer is cord compression until proven otherwise. Image the whole spine because many patients have more than one level.

steps.label: Grade
steps.caption: Sagittal T2 MRI of the thoracic spine in another patient: a pathologic fracture with epidural tumor compressing the cord. Kuah T et al., Cancers 2022 (PMC9265325), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: MRI shows a T8 metastasis with epidural tumor compressing the cord, with no CSF visible around it. What is the Bilsky grade?
steps.explanation: Grade 3 is cord compression with no CSF visible. Grade 2 still shows some CSF around a compressed cord; grade 1 touches the thecal sac without deforming the cord.

steps.label: Predictor
steps.prompt: What is the strongest predictor of whether she will walk after treatment?
choices: Whether she can walk before treatment
steps.explanation: Patients who walk in usually walk out. Speed matters because ambulatory status is lost quickly.

steps.label: Surgery or RT
steps.prompt: She can still walk with help, the compression is at one level, she has bone-only disease, and the spine surgeon thinks she can tolerate surgery. What is the best plan?
choices: Decompressive surgery and stabilization, then radiation
steps.explanation: For a fit patient with single-level compression and a good prognosis, surgery followed by RT keeps more patients walking. Breast cancer is fairly radiosensitive, so RT alone is also reasonable for patients who can't have surgery.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that surgery followed by RT kept more patients walking than RT alone?
steps.explanation: Patchell (2005): in selected patients with single-area compression from non-radiosensitive tumors, 84% walked after surgery plus RT versus 57% after RT alone.

steps.label: Postoperative RT
steps.prompt: She has surgery. What postoperative course would you offer, and when?
steps.answer: A multifraction course such as 30 Gy in 10 (or 20 Gy in 5) to the operated levels and hardware, starting once the wound has healed, usually within a few weeks.
steps.explanation: Her bone-only breast cancer may give her years, which favors longer courses with better local control.

cases.title: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm
cases.oneLiner: A 67-year-old retired carpenter has firm, slowly growing nodules in his right palm at the base of the ring finger for 8 months. They're tender when he grips tools.

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.prompt: Exam shows two palmar nodules and a short cord, and he can lay his hand flat on the table. What is the diagnosis?
steps.explanation: Dupuytren disease starts with nodules in the palmar fascia, then cords, then flexion contracture, most often of the ring and little fingers. A negative tabletop test means no significant contracture yet.

steps.label: Role of RT
steps.prompt: Why is radiation reasonable now and not later?
choices: RT is only for recurrence after surgery
RT works on the proliferating fibroblasts of early disease, slowing progression; it can't straighten a finger once a mature cord has formed
RT is used only for the foot
steps.explanation: The key word for Dupuytren radiation is early. Established contractures need needle aponeurotomy, collagenase, or surgery.

steps.label: Regimen
steps.prompt: What is a typical regimen and technique?
steps.answer: About 30 Gy given as two courses of 5 x 3 Gy separated by 6-12 weeks (or 21 Gy in 7), with orthovoltage X-rays or electrons to the nodules and cords plus a 1-2 cm margin, shielding the rest of the hand.
steps.explanation: The same approach treats Ledderhose disease of the sole.

steps.label: Counseling
steps.prompt: What side effects and risks do you discuss?
steps.answer: Mild redness and dry skin during treatment; later, dry or thin skin or reduced sweating in a few patients. A very small lifetime risk of a radiation-induced cancer, which is lower at his age and in the hand.
steps.explanation: Benign radiation is offered after weighing age, site, and alternatives.

steps.label: Five years later
steps.prompt: Five years later his left ring finger is fixed at 50 degrees of flexion. What do you recommend?
choices: Refer to hand surgery for needle aponeurotomy, collagenase, or fasciectomy
steps.explanation: A fixed contracture is beyond what radiation can fix.

cases.title: Case 4: Before the Second Hip
cases.oneLiner: A 69-year-old man is scheduled for a right total hip replacement next week. Two years ago, after his left hip replacement, bone grew in the soft tissue around the joint and he lost much of his range of motion.

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.prompt: What happened after his first operation?
steps.explanation: Heterotopic ossification is bone forming in soft tissue, most often around the hip after arthroplasty or acetabular fracture surgery.

steps.label: Risk
steps.prompt: What is the strongest risk factor for heterotopic ossification after his second hip replacement?
steps.explanation: Prior HO is the strongest predictor. Others: ankylosing spondylitis, DISH, hypertrophic osteoarthritis, and male sex.

steps.label: Regimen and timing
steps.prompt: What radiation do you offer, and when?
steps.answer: A single 7-8 Gy to the hip, within about 24 hours before surgery or within 72 hours after.
steps.explanation: Radiation kills the precursor cells before they become bone-forming cells, which happens in the first few days. Once bone has formed, radiation can't remove it.

steps.label: Technique
steps.prompt: His new prosthesis will be uncemented, with a porous coating. What do you do?
choices: Shield the porous components so bone can still grow into them
steps.explanation: Uncemented implants rely on bone ingrowth for fixation, so those surfaces are blocked from the field.

steps.label: Alternative
steps.prompt: What is the main non-radiation alternative?
steps.explanation: NSAIDs prevent HO too, but carry GI bleeding and kidney risks and require weeks of dosing.

cases.title: Case 5: It Hurts to Stand
cases.oneLiner: A 56-year-old woman with ER-positive breast cancer, metastatic to bone only, has 3 weeks of left thigh pain that is much worse when she bears weight.

steps.label: Red flag
steps.prompt: Which feature of her pain worries you most?
choices: It is worse with weight bearing
steps.explanation: Functional pain (pain with weight bearing) in a long bone suggests impending fracture. Keep her off the leg until orthopedics weighs in.

steps.label: Score it
steps.prompt: X-rays show a lytic lesion in the femoral shaft involving more than two-thirds of the bone's width. Calculate the Mirels score.
steps.answer: Lower limb 2 + functional pain 3 + lytic 3 + more than 2/3 of the width 3 = 11.
steps.explanation: Site (upper 1, lower 2, peritrochanteric 3), pain (mild 1, moderate 2, functional 3), lesion (blastic 1, mixed 2, lytic 3), width (under 1/3: 1, 1/3-2/3: 2, over 2/3: 3).

steps.label: Next step
steps.prompt: What is the next step?
choices: Orthopedic referral for prophylactic fixation, then postoperative RT
8 Gy in 1 and resume normal activity
steps.explanation: A Mirels score of 9 or more means high fracture risk. Fixing the bone before it breaks is much easier than fixing a fracture.

steps.label: Postoperative RT
steps.prompt: She has an intramedullary rod placed. What postoperative RT do you plan?
steps.answer: A multifraction course (for example 20 Gy in 5 or 30 Gy in 10) to the entire length of the rod, once the wound allows.
steps.explanation: The rod passes through the whole canal and can seed tumor along its length. Postoperative RT improves function and lowers the chance of a second operation.

steps.label: Why longer
steps.prompt: Why not a single 8 Gy fraction here?
choices: Her bone-only breast cancer may give her years, and she needs durable local control so the hardware doesn't fail
steps.explanation: Single fractions are excellent for uncomplicated lesions and short prognosis. After fixation, with a long expected survival, most clinicians use a multifraction course.

cases.title: Case 6: A Tight Collar
cases.oneLiner: A 61-year-old man who smokes has 2 weeks of facial swelling, a feeling that his shirt collars are too tight, and dilated veins over his upper chest. He is breathing comfortably and is alert.

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.prompt: CT shows a large right mediastinal mass compressing the superior vena cava. What is the syndrome, and what is the most common cause?
steps.explanation: Most malignant SVC syndrome comes from lung cancer (especially small cell) and lymphoma. Catheter-related thrombosis is a growing benign cause.

steps.label: Emergency?
steps.prompt: Which finding would make this a true emergency?
steps.explanation: Stridor (laryngeal edema) and confusion (cerebral edema) are the dangerous signs. Most patients have collateral veins and are not in immediate danger.

steps.label: Next step
steps.prompt: He is stable. What is the next step?
choices: Get tissue (biopsy) to make a diagnosis
steps.explanation: Radiating before a biopsy can make the pathology unreadable, and the diagnosis changes the treatment: small cell lung cancer, lymphoma, and germ cell tumors are treated with chemotherapy first.

steps.label: Fast relief
steps.prompt: If he worsened before results came back, what gives the fastest relief?
steps.explanation: A stent relieves symptoms within hours to a day or two; radiation takes 1-2 weeks or more.

steps.label: Pathology
steps.prompt: The biopsy shows small cell lung cancer, limited to the chest. What is the treatment plan?
steps.answer: Platinum-etoposide chemotherapy with early concurrent thoracic radiation (limited-stage small cell), with immunotherapy consolidation and brain imaging and follow-up.
steps.explanation: Small cell responds quickly to chemotherapy, and his SVC symptoms will likely improve within days of starting it.

cases.title: Case 7: Brushing Her Teeth
cases.oneLiner: A 71-year-old woman has 2 years of sudden, electric shock-like pain in her right cheek and jaw lasting a few seconds. It is triggered by brushing her teeth, chewing, and cold wind.

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.prompt: Her neurologic exam is normal between attacks. What is the diagnosis?
steps.explanation: Brief, triggered, electric shock-like pain in the V2/V3 distribution with a normal exam is classic trigeminal neuralgia.

steps.label: Workup
steps.prompt: What imaging do you want, and what would make you think of a different cause in a younger patient?
choices: MRI with thin-slice sequences; bilateral symptoms or young age suggesting multiple sclerosis
steps.explanation: MRI excludes a tumor or MS plaque and often shows a vessel (usually the superior cerebellar artery) compressing the nerve near the pons.

steps.label: First line
steps.prompt: What is the first-line treatment?
steps.explanation: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) controls pain in most patients at first. Procedures are for pain that drugs no longer control or side effects that can't be tolerated.

steps.label: Procedure
steps.prompt: Carbamazepine now makes her dizzy and confused, and she takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Which procedure fits her best?
steps.explanation: SRS is noninvasive and doesn't require stopping anticoagulation, which suits an older patient on a blood thinner. Microvascular decompression is most durable but needs a craniotomy.

steps.label: Dose and target
steps.prompt: Describe the target and dose.
steps.answer: A single 4 mm shot to the trigeminal nerve root in the cistern, a few millimeters in front of the pons, with a maximum dose of about 70-90 Gy (often about 80 Gy) in one session.
steps.explanation: The dose is prescribed to the center of the tiny target, not to its edge.

steps.label: Counseling
steps.prompt: What do you tell her about timing and side effects?
steps.answer: Relief is delayed, usually starting within about 1-3 months, so she should keep her medicine until then. The main side effect is facial numbness or tingling in a minority of patients. Pain can return over years, and SRS can be repeated.
steps.explanation: Outcomes are reported with the BNI pain score.

cases.title: Case 8: A Seizure at Work
cases.oneLiner: A 26-year-old man has a first seizure at work. CT in the emergency department shows a small hemorrhage in the left thalamus.

steps.label: Workup
steps.prompt: MRI shows a tangle of flow voids around the hemorrhage. What test best defines the lesion?
steps.explanation: Angiography is the gold standard for an AVM: it maps the feeding arteries, the nidus, and the draining veins.

steps.label: Grade
steps.prompt: Angiography shows a 2.4 cm AVM in the left thalamus with deep venous drainage. What is the Spetzler-Martin grade?
steps.answer: Size under 3 cm (1) + eloquent location (1) + deep venous drainage (1) = grade III.
steps.explanation: Grades I-II usually go to surgery. Small, deep, or eloquent AVMs are the classic radiosurgery cases.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: It has already bled. Which treatment fits best?
steps.explanation: A ruptured AVM is usually treated because the risk of rebleeding is highest early. A small thalamic AVM is high risk for surgery, so SRS is a good option.

steps.label: Dose
steps.prompt: What SRS dose would you expect?
steps.answer: About 16-25 Gy to the margin of the nidus in one session, often around 18-22 Gy.
steps.explanation: Higher doses close more AVMs but cause more injury to surrounding brain, especially in eloquent areas.

steps.label: Latency
steps.prompt: He asks when he will be protected from another bleed. What do you tell him?
choices: Not until the AVM is completely closed, which usually takes 1-3 years
steps.explanation: The vessels close slowly. Until obliteration is confirmed by angiography, usually around 3 years, the bleeding risk remains.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: His cousin has an unruptured AVM found by chance. Which trial found that medical management alone did better than intervention for unruptured AVMs over its follow-up?
steps.explanation: ARUBA was stopped early when the intervention arm had more strokes and deaths. It is debated (short follow-up, few surgeries), but it made observation a real option for unruptured AVMs.

cases.title: Case 9: Nothing Hurts Yet
cases.oneLiner: A 58-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma, responding well to chemo-immunotherapy, has new bone metastases on restaging. None of them hurt. ECOG 1.

steps.label: Which lesions
steps.prompt: He has a 3.5 cm lesion in the left acetabulum, a lesion in the posterior elements at T12-L1, and several small rib lesions. Which lesions put him at high risk for a skeletal-related event?
choices: The bulky acetabular lesion and the junctional T12-L1 lesion
steps.explanation: Bulky lesions (2 cm or more), hip, shoulder, or sacroiliac joint involvement, junctional spine levels, and posterior vertebral involvement mark high-risk lesions.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that radiating asymptomatic high-risk bone metastases reduced skeletal-related events and hospitalizations and improved survival?
steps.explanation: The Gillespie randomized phase II trial: skeletal-related events fell from about 29% to about 2%. Larger trials are confirming it.

steps.label: Plan
steps.prompt: What is reasonable now?
choices: Radiate every lesion including the ribs
Prophylactic RT to the acetabular and T12-L1 lesions, continuing systemic therapy
steps.explanation: Treat the lesions likely to cause trouble and leave small, low-risk rib lesions alone. Systemic therapy continues.

steps.label: Six months later
steps.prompt: Six months later, everything is controlled except two growing lung nodules. Nothing else is active on PET. What is this pattern called, and what might you offer?
steps.answer: Oligoprogression: SBRT to the progressing sites while continuing the systemic therapy that is controlling everything else.
steps.explanation: CURB showed a progression-free survival benefit for SBRT to oligoprogressive NSCLC, but not breast cancer.

steps.label: Oligometastases
steps.prompt: Which randomized phase II trial showed that SABR to up to 5 metastases, with a controlled primary, improved overall survival?
steps.explanation: SABR-COMET improved overall survival but had a small rate of treatment-related death. NRG-BR002 found no benefit in oligometastatic breast cancer.

cases.title: Case 10: What Are You Hoping For?
cases.oneLiner: A 79-year-old woman with metastatic squamous cell lung cancer, progressing after two lines of therapy, is admitted with daily hemoptysis (a few tablespoons a day) and shortness of breath. She spends most of the day in bed.

steps.label: Prognosis
steps.prompt: What is her ECOG performance status, and what does it suggest?
choices: ECOG 3; likely weeks to a few months
steps.explanation: In bed more than half the day is ECOG 3. Performance status is the most useful single predictor of survival, and clinicians tend to overestimate survival.

steps.label: First conversation
steps.prompt: What is the most useful first question in the room?
choices: "What are you hoping this treatment will do for you?"
steps.explanation: Start with her goals and understanding. Her answer decides whether to treat at all, and how.

steps.label: Course
steps.prompt: She wants the bleeding to stop so she can go home with hospice. Bronchoscopy shows no critical airway obstruction. What do you offer?
choices: A short hemostatic course, such as 10 Gy in 1 or 17 Gy in 2 a week apart
steps.explanation: Short palliative courses control hemoptysis in most patients, often within days, with little toxicity. One fraction fits her prognosis best.

steps.label: Side effects
steps.prompt: What side effects do you warn her about?
steps.answer: Temporary painful swallowing (esophagitis) starting about 1-2 weeks after treatment, fatigue, and a brief flare of cough or chest discomfort.
steps.explanation: Even short courses through the mediastinum can cause esophagitis; offer a numbing mouthwash and soft foods.

steps.label: Hospice
steps.prompt: The hospice team asks whether radiation means she can't enroll. What is the best answer?
choices: She must finish all treatment before hospice
A single palliative fraction doesn't need to delay hospice, and many hospices can coordinate it
steps.explanation: Palliative radiation aimed at comfort fits within hospice goals. Starting long courses near the end of life usually adds burden without benefit.
